The Splitnose rockfish, Sebastes diploproa, is a relatively long-lived scorpaenid found along the continental slope of the North Pacific. Field surveys indicate that individuals typically attain a total length of 46 centimeters [Li = 46 centimeters] at the upper end of their asymptotic growth trajectory. This ultimate length is derived from empirical length-at-age data and represents the maximum size reached by the oldest members of the population. The species exhibits a deep-bodied morphology, with older adults routinely exceeding the one-meter mark in girth, though their length distribution suggests a relatively slow, sustained growth pattern characteristic of many deep-water Sebastes species. Length-frequency analyses from bottom trawl surveys off the coast of Oregon and Washington consistently show that few individuals surpass this 46 centimeter threshold, suggesting a strong asymptotic constraint comparable to that of other mid-depth rockfishes such as Sebastes entomelas, though considerably smaller than the giant Sebastes borealis.

Sexual maturation in the Splitnose rockfish is marked by a distinct body size at the onset of gonadal development. Histological examination of captured specimens indicates that puberty is attained at a total length of 19 centimeters [Lp = 19 centimeters]. This size threshold, derived from the macroscopic examination of ovarian and testicular tissues, corresponds to the length at which 50 percent of the population becomes reproductively active. Fish below this length are invariably immature, possessing undifferentiated gonads, while those exceeding 19 centimeters [Lp = 19 centimeters] show clear signs of vitellogenesis or spermatogenesis during the spawning season. The transition to adulthood occurs after several years of slow somatic growth, a pattern typical of many iteroparous rockfishes that prioritize structural development before reproductive investment begins. This length-based maturity schedule is a critical parameter for stock assessment models aimed at forecasting recruitment dynamics in the face of variable oceanographic conditions.

Reproductive output in Sebastes diploproa is strongly influenced by ambient temperature, with laboratory holding experiments revealing that females achieve a maximum rate of approximately 700 larvae per day [Ri = approximately 700 larvae per day] when maintained at 5.9 °C [T = 5.9 °C]. This rate, recorded from captive gravid females held in flow-through seawater tanks under controlled thermal conditions mimicking their native upwelling habitat, translates to an annual larval production of about 255,000 larvae over a spawning season [Ri = about 255,000 larvae over a spawning season]. The high larval output is an adaptation to the extreme pelagic mortality faced by yolk-sac larvae during their prolonged drift phase. Each female may extrude multiple broods over the spawning period, with the energetic investment being considerable given that larvae are born live following a viviparous gestation. The thermal sensitivity of this reproductive rate is a key consideration for predicting how warming ocean temperatures might alter population productivity and recruitment success.

The neonatal weight of newly extruded larvae is remarkably small, reflecting the extreme energetic cost of producing numerous live offspring. Direct measurements of recently born larvae indicate an individual wet weight of approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams], a value derived from the diameter of the ovulated egg which averages 0.8 millimeters. This minuscule birth mass, consistent with a voluminous larval output, is among the smallest recorded for any Sebastes species, highlighting the trade-off between offspring size and fecundity. The pregnant female invests heavily in gestation but produces endotrophic larvae that rely on their internal yolk reserves for the first several days before transitioning to exogenous feeding on copepod nauplii. The wet weight at puberty, estimated from the length-weight relationship of field-sampled fish, is 89.4 grams [Wwp = 89.4 grams], providing a benchmark for the physical condition necessary to support the energetic demands of first reproduction.

Asymptotic adult body mass in Sebastes diploproa, estimated using the empirical length-weight conversion factor of 0.01000 applied to the cube of ultimate length, reaches a maximum of 1,400 grams [Wwi = 1,400 grams]. This value is consistent with the largest individuals retrieved from deep-water longline sets off the coast of British Columbia. At the thermal conditions typical of their deep benthic habitat, averaging 5.9 °C [T = 5.9 °C], the species exhibits a life span of approximately 86 years [am = approximately 86 years], making it one of the longer-lived members of its genus. The oldest documented individual, aged through otolith annuli analysis, reached this value, confirming the extreme longevity characteristic of many slow-growing deep-sea fishes. This extended lifespan, combined with delayed maturity and low fecundity, renders the population particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as recovery times are measured in decades rather than years.
